title: Gilles Villeneuve Biopic Charts the Rise of a Legend

body_markdown:
“If someone said to me that you can have three wishes, my first would have been to get into racing, my second to be in Formula 1, my third to drive for Ferrari…”


These words from Canada’s greatest racer, Gilles Villeneuve, are a neat synopsis of a new biopic about his early life. *Villeneuve: Rise of a Legend* is a family project, with Villeneuve’s daughter Melanie serving as Executive Producer, and done with the support of 1997 F1 World Champion son Jacques.


As Gilles chased his dreams, which took him from local snowmobile races to the international stage, his family was alongside him. At one point, as documented in the film, Gilles even sold the family home—without telling his wife Joann—to fund his next step on the racing ladder.


“We didn’t really know life any other way,” says Melanie Villeneuve. “We started traveling in a motorhome. I was three, and my brother was five. We went from track to track in North America on the Formula Atlantic circuit, living on the road. It was a way for him to have a family life, and for my mom to be close to her husband and for the kids to be involved. We loved it! We enjoyed ourselves; those years were amazing.”


“Most memories I have of my father are of either racing or doing something else where he was pushing to the limit; whether it was on skis, or driving his pick-up truck, or flying the chopper,” continues Jacques Villeneuve. “But my earliest memories go back to when we lived in a trailer on blocks across the road from my grandparents’ house in Berthierville. If I think about it now, I wouldn’t want to live there. But back then, it felt fun.”


Villeneuve Family


Born in Quebec in 1950, Gilles inherited a gift for music from his piano-tuning father, but chose to pursue a different kind of performance. At 15, he rebuilt a 1958 MGA, and later modified his 1967 Ford Mustang for the track. That car is still in the family—and the movie.


In the winter months, he raced snowmobiles, earning enough prize money to buy his first single-seater race car: a used Formula Ford. It was two years older and obsolete compared to the cars his competitors drove, but Villeneuve still won seven out of ten races and took the local championship title in 1973.


To move up to Formula Atlantic the following year, Villeneuve sold his home, much to Joann’s displeasure. At Mosport Park, he crashed and broke his leg, but was undeterred, winning his first race in 1975, and then the U.S. and Canadian championships in 1976.


Rémi Goulet as Gilles Villeneuve


Christal Films


During the race at Trois-Rivières, Villeneuve found himself up against F1 drivers James Hunt and Alan Jones, beating them both. “I went over there and got thrashed,” recalled Hunt. “You didn’t have to be much of a brain surgeon to spot his talent.”


Magnanimously, Hunt even persuaded McLaren boss Teddy Mayer to give Villeneuve his Grand Prix debut at the 1977 British Grand Prix. Driving the previous year’s car, he qualified ahead of teammate Jochen Mass. He finished 11th after a forced pit stop to fix a water temperature issue, but his performance did not go unnoticed.


Enzo Ferrari was watching and hired the Canadian. “When they presented me with this ‘piccolo Canadese,’ this minuscule bundle of nerves, I immediately recognised in him the physique of Nuvolari and said to myself, let’s give him a try,” said Ferrari.


Villeneuve would reward Ferrari with six wins from 66 starts, before tragedy struck at Zolder, Netherlands, in 1982. During qualifying, Villeneuve came over the brow of the hill after the first chicane to find a slow-moving Jochen Mass in his path. Mass tried to move out of the way, but Villeneuve also steered right, and the two cars collided. The Ferrari was launched into the air and disintegrated on hitting the ground. Villeneuve was thrown into the catch fencing, his neck broken. Despite the best efforts of medics and fellow drivers John Watson and Derek Warwick, who were first on the scene, Villeneuve was declared dead at 21:12 European time on May 8, 1982.


It’s a day that Québécois film director Yan Lanouette Turgeon will never forget. “I remember May 8th, 1982, the day Gilles died. I remember my parents, where I was, the feeling in the house when we heard the news. When I came on board a couple of years ago to direct this film, the day I shook producer Christian Larouche’s hand to commit was May 8th. When I told him the significance of this date, his hair stood on end. We were like, okay, maybe it’s a sign. This is a movie that’s been in the making for a long time. It has been in development for ten years. My feeling from the get-go, as soon as I was involved in the project, was that Gilles Villeneuve’s story needs to be told. He was such an interesting character. He remains a monumental figure in Quebec and in Formula One, and a movie had never been made about him. I felt I needed to be the one to make this movie, and the timing is perfect as interest in Formula One has never been greater.”


Christal Films


For Melanie Villeneuve, the film has been in the making for much longer. It’s a full 12 years since she first began discussions. “When I started on this journey, I was trying to understand where my dad sits in the public space,” she explains. “There was *Senna* , and there was *Rush* , Ron Howard’s film about James Hunt and Niki Lauda. I began thinking: Why isn’t there something like that for Gilles? I wanted to make sure his memory survived, and that it survived through us as a family rather than a third party. It was time to reclaim a little bit of that heritage.”


“Watching the trailer, it was difficult to hold back the tears,” says Jacques. “And I love that it focuses on the early years, the years no one but our family knows about. Most biopics focus on when someone’s in their prime, and they tend to rush through or gloss over how they got there. They give the audience what they already know, whereas this film shows the building blocks.”


“The film is squeezing about 10 years of his life into two hours,” adds Melanie. “But it sets out to showcase exactly that: How does a lower-middle-class guy from very rural Quebec—where there’s hockey, then more hockey and no one cared about racing—become Enzo Ferrari’s favourite driver? Because he had a vision. He was a man on a mission, taking one step forward every single day. It’s a story about passion and perseverance.”


*Villeneuve: Rise of a Legend* premieres at the Toronto International Film Festival on September 19 and will hit theaters in Quebec in November, with a global launch in 2027—50 years since Villeneuve’s F1 debut.
